Short answer
- Root cause: the single cache pod (Service: shop/cache -> Pod: cache-9ffcf47fc-5d4xf) is saturated — it hits its max active-connections limit (40) and a large queued backlog (150), so cache requests from checkout-api time out (2s client timeout).

Key evidence (exact resources, times)
- checkout-api logs (namespace shop) show repeated timeouts to the cache service:
  - Example lines (filtered logs, last hour): "2026-10-07T09:05:11Z ERROR checkout-api cache GET cart:9366 timed out after 2.0s (cache:6379) [TimeoutError]" — many similar entries between ~09:05 and 09:15.
- cache service & endpoints:
  - Service: shop/cache → CLUSTER-IP 10.96.204.9 port 6379 (selector app=cache).
  - Endpoint(s) backing service "cache": 10.244.3.2 → Pod: shop/cache-9ffcf47fc-5d4xf.
- cache pod logs (shop/cache-9ffcf47fc-5d4xf) show saturation:
  - "cache-server starting log_level=debug max_active=40"
  - Repeated lines showing connection table saturation and growing queue:
    - e.g. "2026-10-07T09:14:58Z conn-table active=40/40 queued=63 ..."
    - peak observed: "2026-10-07T09:15:28Z conn-table active=40/40 queued=141" then "queued=150" continuing after that.
  - These log lines show the cache has reached max_active=40 and queued requests rising into the hundreds.
- NetworkPolicy exists but allows checkout-api:
  - NetworkPolicy "cache-ingress" selects app=cache and allows ingress from pods with label tier=backend. checkout-api pods have label tier=backend, so policy is not blocking traffic.

Why (concise five-whys)
1. Why do checkout-api calls time out? Because cache GETs are timing out (2s client timeout).
2. Why are cache GETs timing out? Because the cache server is not responding quickly — requests are queued.
3. Why are requests queued? Because the cache process has reached its max_active connection limit (40).
4. Why is the limit being hit? Because many clients/connections are contacting the single cache pod (connection counts in cache logs show many peer IPs and ~40 active connections constantly; queued backlog grows).
5. Why a single pod? The service has only one endpoint (only one cache pod), so all traffic funnels to one instance and becomes a bottleneck.

Immediate mitigation (safe, concrete commands)
1. Scale cache to >1 replica (quickest mitigation):
   - kubectl scale deployment cache -n shop --replicas=3
   If your cache is not a Deployment named "cache" adjust to the correct resource (kubectl get deployment -n shop).
2. Increase cache's concurrency limit (env var MAX_ACTIVE) and rollout:
   - kubectl set env deployment/cache MAX_ACTIVE=200 -n shop
   - kubectl rollout restart deployment/cache -n shop
3. As a short term client-side safety, raise checkout-api cache timeout or add retries/backoff (in app config) to avoid tight 2s failures while scaling completes.

Commands I ran / data I examined
- kubectl get pods -n shop (identified checkout-api and cache pods)
- kubectl logs -n shop checkout-api-58f9d6b876-<pod> (fetched checkout-api errors; saw many TimeoutError lines)
- kubectl get svc cache -n shop (cache service info: ClusterIP 10.96.204.9:6379)
- kubectl get endpoints cache -n shop (single endpoint 10.244.3.2 -> cache-9ffcf47fc-5d4xf)
- kubectl logs -n shop cache-9ffcf47fc-5d4xf (cache logs showing max_active=40 and queued growing to 150)
- kubectl get networkpolicies -n shop (cache-ingress allows tier=backend pods → checkout-api allowed)

Notes / caveats
- I observed only one cache pod behind the service. If your intended design was a single-instance cache (for correctness), consider whether that design can handle peak load or if you should place a fronting load-balancer/redis cluster.
- The cache logs show which peer IPs hold many connections (e.g., 10.244.1.4, 10.244.3.5, etc.). You can map those pod IPs to pod names to find which client(s) are heavy:
  - kubectl get pods -o wide -n shop | grep <IP>
  - kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces | grep <IP>
- I could not run pod exec probes from outside (kubectl run / kubectl exec variants require additional approvals here). The diagnosis above is based on the logs and resource state I fetched.

Recommended next steps (short and mid term)
1. Short term (0–10 minutes)
   - Scale cache replicas to 3 and/or increase MAX_ACTIVE so requests are served instead of queued.
   - Temporarily increase client timeout and add retry/backoff in checkout-api (to avoid immediate user-facing errors while cache scales).
2. Mid term (hours)
   - Make cache horizontally scalable (replicas + sticky/session design if needed) or move to a managed Redis cluster.
   - Add metrics/alerts: connection count, queue depth, rejected connections; alert when active == max_active and queue > threshold.
   - Investigate client behavior: map IPs from cache log "peers=..." to pods to find the high-connection clients and fix connection churn/leaks (use connection pooling instead of creating many short-lived connections).
3. Long term
   - Capacity plan: determine expected max concurrent connections and set MAX_ACTIVE and replica count accordingly.
   - Implement readiness/liveness probes and more robust load distribution if stateful.

If you want, I can:
- Run commands to map the peer IPs shown in the cache logs to specific pods (kubectl get pods -o wide -n ... and grep) — tell me if I should run those.
- Propose exact rollout patches (Deployment YAML snippets) to scale cache and change MAX_ACTIVE and show a safe rollback plan.
